name: QuAC
summary: 7,354 questions from 1,000 crowdsourced dialogues in which a student asked about a Wikipedia section they could not see and a teacher answered with spans of it, or marked the question unanswerable.
overview:
QuAC is a dataset of information-seeking dialogues. Each dialogue pairs two crowdworkers in a chatroom: a student who sees only the title of a Wikipedia article and a short summary of it, and a teacher who sees one section of that article. The student asks questions to learn about the hidden section, and the teacher may answer only by selecting a span of the section text, so every answer is a quotation rather than a sentence the teacher wrote. Alongside each span the teacher records two dialog acts, an affirmation for yes-or-no questions and a continuation signal saying whether the student should, could, or should not keep on this line of questioning, and may mark a question unanswerable from the section. The release holds 98,407 questions in 13,594 dialogues over 8,854 sections of 3,611 articles, and was published in August 2018 with a paper at EMNLP. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07036)

Asking without seeing the text is what makes the questions unlike reading-comprehension questions. They are short, averaging 6.5 words, and they lean on what came before: in the authors' sample of 100 questions, 86% could not be understood without the dialogue context, 61% referred to the subject of the article and 44% to an entity or event introduced earlier in the conversation. Because the student is guessing at what the section contains, about a fifth of the questions cannot be answered from it at all, and a dialogue was cut short once three unanswerable questions had been asked, or once it reached twelve questions. A model therefore has to resolve references against the conversation, find a span, decide when no span will do, and predict the two dialog acts. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07036)

The gap to people has narrowed but not closed. The authors' best reference model, a BiDAF++ reader given the two previous answers, reached 60.1 F1 on the hidden test set against 81.1 for a human annotator, and matched human F1 on every question of only 4.0% of dialogues. The strongest submission on the leaderboard, an ensemble from Ant Group recorded in August 2022, reaches 76.3 F1 and matches human F1 on 73.6% of questions, yet still does so for every question of just 17.9% of dialogues, where a person manages 100%. Sustaining a whole dialogue remains much harder than answering one question well. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07036) and [leaderboard](https://quac.ai/)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete official validation split, the published file `val_v0.2.json`: 1,000 dialogues, one per section, holding 7,354 questions about 1,000 sections of 721 Wikipedia articles, where 462 articles contribute one section, 242 two, 14 three, and 3 four. The training split of 83,568 questions over 6,843 sections is not imported, and the 7,353-question test split is not public at all: researchers submit a model to the leaderboard, which runs it on the hidden set. The authors publish the data as plain files with no version history, so this snapshot pins the file by its SHA-256 digest; the copy behind that digest was uploaded in October 2018. [Validation split](https://s3.amazonaws.com/my89public/quac/val_v0.2.json)

Each Task Prompt opens with the question, then gives the earlier turns of its dialogue, the article and section titles, the summary of the article the student was shown, and the full section text the teacher read, each reproduced verbatim. The history is written as Student and Teacher lines carrying the answer the original teacher gave during collection, which is what the student had seen when asking the next question. The section text ends with the word CANNOTANSWER, which the dataset appends to every section so that the teacher's "no answer" can itself be a span; it is kept as upstream wrote it, and no instruction is added telling a model what to do with it. Section texts run from 251 to 1,584 words, averaging 440; 85 of the 1,000 are longer than the 550-word ceiling the authors' datasheet describes. Dialogues run from 4 to 12 questions, most often 8.

The Solution lists every reference answer recorded for the question, one per line in upstream order. The validation split carries up to five references per question, gathered in a separate task where one worker answered the pre-recorded student questions: 3,953 questions have five, 2,086 have four, 1,175 have three, 132 have two, and 8 have one. Annotators often chose the same span, and those repeats are kept because the official F1 is computed over the reference set as recorded. For the 1,486 questions where every reference is CANNOTANSWER, a single CANNOTANSWER line is written, as the official script does with such a question; no question in this split mixes the marker with real spans. Two further lines give the affirmation, which is yes for 1,500 questions, no for 122, and neither for 5,732, and the continuation signal, which is follow up for 4,255, maybe follow up for 1,358, and do not follow up for 1,741. Keys are the upstream question identifiers, such as `C_a2ccac6e089341c98a43b7e9a936bd60_0_q#3`, which number the questions of a dialogue from zero; in one dialogue the numbering skips a number, and this snapshot keeps the identifiers as recorded rather than renumbering them.

Every article is credited. QuAC records the title of each article and section but not the revision its text came from, so the ATTRIBUTION.md the importer regenerates lists all 721 articles with links to them as they stand now, and each prompt names the article and section it quotes. Prompt and solution links point at the published split file, which has no per-question addresses. The importer uses only Python's standard library, checks every reference span against the recorded offset in the section text, and can be rerun with python3 data/quac/import.py.
scoring:
A model answers each question in turn with a span of the section text, or with CANNOTANSWER, and also predicts the two dialog acts. The official script scores a prediction by word-level F1 against the references, after lowercasing, dropping punctuation and the articles a, an, and the, and collapsing whitespace. With n references it averages, over the n subsets that leave one reference out, the best F1 the prediction achieves against that subset, which is also how it measures a human annotator: the human F1 for a question is how well one reference matches the others. Questions whose human F1 falls below 40 are left out of the headline F1, which removes roughly the noisiest 10% of annotations, and the script reports an unfiltered F1 over all questions beside it. [Official script](https://s3.amazonaws.com/my89public/quac/scorer.py)

Two further metrics ask whether a model reaches a person's level. HEQ-Q is the share of questions where the model's F1 matches or exceeds the human F1, and HEQ-D is the share of dialogues where that holds for every question in the dialogue, so one weak turn loses the whole dialogue. The script also reports accuracy on the affirmation and continuation labels and the F1 on just the unanswerable questions, where a prediction scores only if it is exactly CANNOTANSWER. Leaderboard numbers come from running a submitted model on the hidden test set; numbers computed on this validation split are self-reported and are not comparable with them. [Project page](https://quac.ai/)

Benchopedia stores the questions, the dialogue history, the section text, the reference spans, and the dialog acts. It does not run the official script or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The articles are a deliberately narrow slice of Wikipedia. The authors filtered to articles about people in a handful of categories, then kept only popular ones, because pilot workers found it easier to ask about people than about arbitrary topics. By the authors' own count, 76% of the articles are about men, 16% about women, and the rest mostly about groups such as bands, while 36% are about musicians, 15% about sports figures, and 13% about film or television personalities. Their datasheet says the dataset is not suited to training general-purpose information-seeking systems and that they do not recommend deploying models trained on it. [Datasheet](https://quac.ai/updated_datasheet.pdf)

The collection design shapes the answers. A teacher could not write free text, only select spans, which the authors chose because span answers can be scored by F1; the dialog acts were added to give back a little of the flexibility a real answerer has. The references in this split come from a different task than the answers in the training data: a single validation worker answered pre-recorded questions at a flat rate per question, while the original teachers earned more for longer dialogues, so validation spans are shorter, 12.3 tokens on average against 15.1 in training. The dialogue history in these prompts shows the original teacher's span, not the validation worker's, because that is what the student actually saw. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07036)

Scoring rewards reproducing the wording a worker happened to pick. A longer span that contains the reference loses F1, and a shorter one that answers the question just as well also loses, which is why the authors score against human agreement rather than against a single gold answer. Unanswerable questions are all-or-nothing: only the exact marker counts. HEQ-D is unforgiving by design, so dialogue-level numbers stay low even for strong models, and the ten percent of questions with low annotator agreement are dropped rather than adjudicated.

The text is a 2018 snapshot of Wikipedia with no revision recorded, so a reader checking an article today may not find the sentence the teacher quoted; 23 of the 721 titles now redirect to a renamed article, two are mangled by an upstream escaping defect, and two section titles still carry the trailing "Edit" of the Wikipedia interface they were scraped from. The split has been public since 2018 and carries no canary string, so a model may have seen these dialogues, sections, and answers in training; only the hidden test set offers a measurement free of that doubt.
